News and Press Release Nueva York/Ginebra, 3 de septiembre de 2026 – La Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media

Luna Roja (IFRC) lanza hoy su nueva campaña mundial, "El tratado que le falta a la Tierra", para mostrar una cruda realidad: mientras que el derecho internacional protege a astronautas en situaciones de peligro, no existe ningún tratado internacional integral que establezca cómo deben cooperar los países para proteger a las personas en casos de desastre.

Un tratado global proporcionaría un marco común para la cooperación internacional antes de que se produzcan los desastres, y en caso de que se necesite ayuda internacional. En la práctica, esto podría traducirse en un despliegue más rápido de los equipos humanitarios, trámites aduaneros y fronterizos más sencillos para los suministros de primera necesidad, una cooperación más predecible entre los gobiernos y las organizaciones humanitarias, menores costos y menos trabas administrativas, así como una mejor protección para las personas afectadas por los desastres.

De forma paralela al lanzamiento de la campaña, la IFRC publica un nuevo análisis global que muestra por qué es necesario un tratado sobre desastres y qué diferencia podría suponer. El estudio recopila datos sobre el riesgo de desastres, la protección y los obstáculos a la ayuda internacional, junto con cuatro estudios de caso de Belice, Fiyi, Líbano y Madagascar.

Lea los estudios de caso de Belice, Fiyi, Líbano y Madagascar.

En 2027, los gobiernos se reunirán para negociar el tratado, y la IFRC pone a su disposición su apoyo a lo largo de todo el proceso, ofreciendo conocimientos técnicos y décadas de experiencia en la preparación y respuesta ante desastres.

She will brief on the launch of the latest UNEP report, called "Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return". The report finds that as global temperatures rise, the world must strive to return to below 1.5°C as soon as possible and simultaneously reduce the vulnerability of societies, communities and economies to climate impacts.

IFRC Disaster Research and Campaign Launch - Press Conference Summary

Hybrid Press Briefing by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) on the new IFRC disaster research and campaign launch: astronauts at the heart of push for world's first international disaster treaty

Description

Briefers (in-person) are:

Dylan Winder, IFRC Permanent Observer to the UN and Director of

Humanitarian Diplomacy and Communications;

Dr Sian Proctor, Geoscientist and astronaut; and

Isabelle Granger, IFRC Global Lead, Disaster Law.

News and Press Release International treaties protect astronauts in distress.

But if a flood strikes your city, there is still no comprehensive global treaty to help countries cut through red tape and coordinate international assistance.

New York/Geneva, 3 September 2026 – The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) is today launching a new global campaign, Earth's Missing Treaty , to highlight a stark reality: while international law protects astronauts in distress, there is no comprehensive international treaty setting out how countries should cooperate to protect people before, during and after disasters.

The campaign highlights IFRC's call for countries to support the adoption of the Treaty on the Protection of Persons in the Event of Disasters, which UN Member States have agreed to negotiate and which would be the first comprehensive global treaty dedicated to protecting people before, during and after disasters.

A global treaty would provide a common framework for international cooperation before disasters strike and when international assistance is needed. In practice, this could mean faster deployment of humanitarian teams, simpler customs and border procedures for life-saving supplies, more predictable cooperation between governments and humanitarian organisations, lower costs and fewer administrative barriers, and better protection for people affected by disasters.

Alongside the campaign, IFRC is publishing new global analysis showing why a disaster treaty is needed and the difference it could make. The research brings together data on disaster risk, protection and barriers to international assistance, alongside four country case studies from Belize, Fiji, Lebanon and Madagascar.

Read the case studies for Belize, Fiji, Lebanon and Madagascar

News and Press Release New York/Genève, le 3 septembre 2026 – La Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du

Croissant-Rouge (IFRC) lance aujourd'hui une nouvelle campagne mondiale, intitulée Earth's Missing Treaty (Le traité manquant de la Terre), afin de mettre en lumière une réalité frappante : alors que le droit international impose une obligation globale de secourir les astronautes en détresse, il n'existe aucun traité international global définissant la manière dont les pays doivent coopérer pour protéger les populations avant, pendant et après une catastrophe.

Cette campagne vient soutenir l'appel de l'IFRC pour que les États s'engagent en faveur de l'adoption du Traité sur la protection des personnes en cas de catastrophe. Actuellement négocié par les États membres de l'ONU, ce texte constitue le tout premier traité mondial d'envergure dédié à la protection des populations face aux crises humanitaires majeures.

Un traité mondial offrirait un cadre commun pour la coopération internationale, aussi bien en amont des catastrophes qu'au moment où l'aide internationale devient nécessaire. En pratique, cela se traduirait par un déploiement plus rapide des équipes humanitaires, des procédures douanières et frontalières simplifiées pour l'acheminement des secours vitaux, une coopération plus prévisible entre les gouvernements et les organisations humanitaires, une réduction des coûts et des barrières administratives, ainsi qu'une meilleure protection des populations touchées par les catastrophes.

Cette année, l'IFRC a publié quatre études de cas analysant l'impact potentiel de ce traité sur la protection des personnes lors de catastrophes au Belize, aux Fidji, au Liban et à Madagascar.

Lire les études de cas pour le Belize, les Fidji, le Liban et Madagascar (en anglais).

Photo caption: Nellie Evison – 2026 UC Master of Laws graduate.

A comparative study by Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) Master of Laws graduate Nellie Evison found that legal protections and emergency response provisions for utility workers after disasters in New Zealand and the United States were often voluntary or not explicit.

“Utility workers are essential to restoring power, water and other critical services after a disaster, and they can face many of the same hazards as emergency responders. Having clear legal protections helps to keep them safe, clarifies responsibilities and supports a faster, more coordinated recovery,” Evison says.

Working with QuakeCoRE, a Centre of Research Excellence that aims to improve earthquake resilience, along with the specialist knowledge Evison developed through her research, have helped launch her career. Before graduating, she secured a Wellington-based role at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) as an advisor in incident management and emergency management.

Evison believes her familiarity with New Zealand's Coordinated Incident Management System was a key factor in gaining her role at MBIE.

“I looked at it a lot during my master's, so the theoretical knowledge I acquired through my research has been directly applicable to what I am doing,” she says.

Her team helps build emergency management and business continuity capability across MBIE and supports incident management teams during local and national responses. Evison has already put her knowledge into practice in the logistics function during responses.

When disaster strikes, strong laws save lives. 

From early warnings to faster humanitarian assistance, the right laws can remove barriers, protect the most vulnerable and ensure no one is left behind.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies is advocating for a global Disaster Law Treaty that puts people first.

Noon briefing of 2 September 2026 CLIMATE REPORT/OVERSHOOT

In a video message on the launch of the latest UN Environment Programme (UNEP) report, called “Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return”, the Secretary-General noted that humanity is speeding past the limit to avoid climate catastrophe. He pointed out that we are set to breach the 1.5 degree limit within the next few years, and this summer's scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead.

The Secretary-General warned that every fraction of a degree will cost lives, will destroy livelihoods, will deepen

inequality and push ecosystems closer to irreversible damage. He stressed that we must make the overshoot as small and short as possible, limiting how high temperatures rise and how long they remain above 1.5, and that the fight for 1.5 degrees is the fight for humanity.

IRAN

The Secretary-General is gravely concerned by the renewed exchanges of fire overnight between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Secretary-General is deeply alarmed by reports of civilian casualties, including in a strike that reportedly hit a wedding ceremony in Iran. The Secretary-General condemns all attacks against civilians. He recalls that all parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution.

As we have seen, few countries in the region are immune from this escalation, with airspace and critical shipping routes continuing to be heavily impacted.

The Secretary-General reiterates his call for an immediate cessation of military action and urges all concerned to exercise restraint and refrain from actions and rhetoric that could further escalate already high tensions.

Further escalation, as you can imagine, would have devastating consequences for civilians and for the wider region
